awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: AI-Accelerate Superconductor Discovery for High-Field Magnets
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this SBIR Phase I project is the development of novel superconducting materials that can be easily manufactured and operate at higher temperatures than those used in today’s commercial systems. Superconductors are critical components in technologies such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and fusion energy, but current materials either require complex manufacturing process and/or ultra-cold operating temperatures limiting their widespread use. This project aims to discover materials that can reduce both cost and complexity of using superconductors. The innovation could dramatically lower the cost of MRI machines and expand their availability in underserved healthcare settings. In the energy sector, these materials could help advance the commercial viability of fusion reactors by improving magnetic confinement efficiency and vastly reducing reactor’s cost. The project addresses a long-standing challenge in a multibillion-dollar market. It also supports national interests by facilitating domestic manufacturing of advanced materials, reducing dependence on scarce resources like helium and improving energy efficiency. The technology, if successful, offers a durable competitive advantage by enabling the in-house discovery and production of new superconducting wires that outperform current market incumbents. The long-term vision includes scaling discovered materials to full wire production and integrating them into next-generation medical and energy systems.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to accelerate the discovery of next-generation superconductors using an AI-accelerated workflow. The technical challenge addressed is the discovery of new superconducting materials that are not only high-performing but also stable, synthesizable, and suitable for industrial manufacturing. The project will use a combination of advanced artificial intelligence models, first-principles simulations, and experimental synthesis to identify compounds with high superconducting transition temperatures and practical manufacturing characteristics. The research will focus on generating a large database of candidate materials, and screening them by predicting critical properties including stability, manufacturability and superconducting properties. A subset of the most promising candidates will be synthesized and experimentally characterized to assess their manufacturability and superconducting performance. The most performant candidates will be formed into a mono-filament wire. These findings will serve as a foundation for developing manufacturable wire prototypes in subsequent work.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Below a critical temperature (Tc), superconductors carry direct current with zero electrical resistance. They can sustain current densities orders of magnitude higher than copper, which lets them generate intense, stable magnetic fields with no resistive losses. These properties could transform medicine, energy, computing and transportation. Today, roughly two-thirds of the world’s population lacks access to MRI, in part because MRI magnets must be kept continuously at cryogenic temperatures, so they draw power even when idle. Fusion power plants are racing toward the grid, but the high-temperature superconducting tape in their magnets degrades rapidly under neutron irradiation. Data centers are scaling quickly, yet copper needs many parallel cables to carry the current they require. And as electrification reaches aviation, copper-wound motors remain too heavy for flight. Better superconductors offer a path through all of these challenges.

Yet the only mature commercial market for superconductors is MRI, which accounts for about 63% of the market. For nearly 40 years, engineers have faced a hard trade-off. Low-temperature superconductors are durable, ductile and easy to manufacture at scale, but they perform modestly and must operate near 4 kelvin, which requires costly cryogenic infrastructure. High-temperature superconductors perform far better, but they are fragile ceramics that are difficult to produce at scale and degrade quickly in demanding environments.

In this Phase I project, Quantum Formatics developed an AI-accelerated discovery platform that shrinks the search for new superconductors from decades to days. We used it to target ductile superconductors that can operate at 10 to 20 kelvin. At the core of the platform is a bootstrapped ensemble of equivariant graph neural networks that predicts superconducting properties from a material’s atomic structure. Over four iterations of this model, we reduced prediction error by nearly 70%.

Using the platform, we screened more than 5 million candidate materials, then synthesized and characterized 108 of them in the laboratory. Eighty were superconducting, and 13 outperformed niobium-titanium, in terms of superconducting critical temperature.

An MRI magnet operating at 20 kelvin would need about 27 times less power for cooling. That would ease the burden of a continuous power supply and could help expand MRI access worldwide. For fusion, ductile superconductors are expected to offer the strongest radiation tolerance of any known class of superconductor, and projections suggest magnets made from them could last the full life of a fusion plant without replacement.

Phase I validated the discovery platform and identified candidate materials to develop into wire. Quantum Formatics will continue advancing both the platform and the materials discovered to date, and is pursuing Phase II funding to carry these superconductors from discovery all the way to wire.
